newsitem.title: USA: Seagram chief wants Time Warner to lower debt.
newsitem.headline: Seagram chief wants Time Warner to lower debt.

text.p: Seagram Co chairman Edgar Bronfman Sr, the third biggest stockholder in Time Warner Inc, says he wants to see the media giant reduce its $18 billion debt as a way to increase the value of its stock.

In an interview with Reuters Television conducted Tuesday night, Bronfman declined comment on what he thought of Time Warner chairman Gerald Levin's handling of the company, but said, "We obviously are disappointed that the stock has not moved the way we think it should have moved."
He added, "I personally think they have too many assets tied up in what I call hardware -- cable and other things -- and not enough in content, (although) they are very big in content."

Bronfman then said he thought the company's real problem is "that they have just too much debt. They can't seem to come up from under the debt. I wish they would come up with a plan, which I think they are trying very hard to do."

The 67-year-old billionaire said he thought Time Warner was working with U S West and others, but added, "I don't know this, but I think it is true. They are trying to make sense out of their balance sheet and when they do this, their stock will appreciate and we will be a happy investor."

Bronfman owns 9.8 percent of Time Warner, while Ted Turner owns 11 percent of the media giant's stock and Liberty Media has a 10 percent non-voting share. A Time Warner spokesman said the company's debt was $18 billion.
In the interview, Bronfman also discussed criticism of Seagrams' Universal Music Group distribution of rap records with controversial lyrics.

Bronfman's son Edgar Jr., who is chief executive officer of Seagrams and its MCA division, was roundly attacked last year by cultural activists because the company put out gangsta rap with objectionable sexual lyrics.
Asked about the criticism, Bronfman Sr said, "Rap music is controversial, but it is what the street wants today. We have been careful about what we issue and don't issue.

"Perhaps we have leaned a little bit too far into agreeing to some things that are not acceptable. But we will learn. Our intentions are that we should not be producing anything that most people find objectionable."
